KEY MESSAGE 1...A frontal boundary south of the region will keep 
rain chances around through mid-week, especially across southern 
portions of the area.

The cold front that crossed through our region Sunday night is 
stalling to our south, and remain there through Tuesday. It 
continues to look like it will lift a little closer to our region 
tonight into Tuesday morning as a warm front, but remain just south 
of the area. Due to the closer proximity, and a mid level short wave 
trough, mean that that period will have the highest chance for rain 
across our region. Given that our low will be on the cool side of 
the front, showers are going to be the main mode of any 
precipitation. However, isolated, embedded thunderstorms will be 
possible over Delmarva, particularly during the day on Tuesday.

Confidence is high that temperatures will be below normal starting 
Tuesday. In fact, temperatures will likely struggle to get out of 
the 60s areawide through most of this week. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...A closed mid-level low ejecting from the Ohio Valley 
is expected to lead to the development of a surface low off the 
Eastern Seaboard during the middle and latter parts of this week. 
Depending on the track of the low, it could bring increased rainfall 
chances to the region. 

Confidence continues to increase that as a mid-level impulse tracks 
eastward out of portions of the Midwest and Ohio Valley towards the 
Eastern Seaboard, surface cyclogenesis will occur off the coast of 
the Carolinas Tuesday into Tuesday night. The initial track of the 
developing low is expected to be to the northeast, well offshore. 
However, with a strong high centered over portions of Quebec, a 
sharp pressure gradient over the region will at least lead to breezy 
conditions through Thursday near the coast. It should remain mostly 
dry through this period however. 

Friday and beyond, significant uncertainty remains. Models now fall 
into two relatively distinct camps, with one camp continuing to take 
the low northeast and away from the region. The other camp has the 
low deviating due northward or even northwestward to our region. The 
EC ensembles are generally clustered fairly tightly near the 
deterministic EC, which would favor this scenario. On the other 
hand, the deterministic GFS has the low continuing northeastward and 
the GEFS only has a few members bringing the low towards the coast.

Unfortunately, the difference in sensible weather outcomes between 
these two scenarios is substantial. Should the low track 
northeastward away from the region, any rain would be confined to 
the immediate coast, if any, and winds would decrease quicker. A 
track closer to the coast or even into the coast would lead to 
potentially significant impacts from rain and wind. For now, PoPs 
are maintained in the 20-40% range, and highest southeast of I-95. 
It is worth noting that there are several members in the ensemble 
suites which feature a middle ground scenario, where the low does 
deviate some but still remains fairly comfortably offshore. This 
scenario would lead to some impacts from rain and wind, but the 
inland extent would be fairly limited. We will continue to monitor 
trends closely as we try to nail down specific impacts and timing 
over the coming days. 


KEY MESSAGE 3...Multiple rounds of potentially significant tidal 
flooding expected for this week. The first batch of Coastal Flood 
headlines have been issued with more likely to come. 

With a slow moving coastal storm increasingly likely, the threat for 
tidal flooding has increased. Strong onshore flow that is projected 
to last for several days will result in water piling up across tidal 
tributaries and within back bays of coastal communities. Tidal 
levels will also be enhanced with astronomical tides increasing with 
the upcoming Full Moon on Saturday. This combination of factors will 
lead to widespread tidal flooding, some of which could get to the 
Moderate stage. While not currently forecast, the threat for major 
flooding is not off the table, especially getting near the full 
moon. 

Minor tidal flooding begins as early as tomorrow afternoon and 
evening for some locations. A Coastal Flood Advisory was issued for 
Ocean, Atlantic, and Cape May County in New Jersey and Kent and 
Sussex County in Delaware. For those same areas, tide levels are 
expected to increase for Wednesday and Thursday, potentially getting 
to Moderate stage. A Coastal Flood Watch was issued for Wednesday 
and Thursday evening's high tide. Moderate tidal flooding could even 
continue into the weekend. As mentioned above, cannot rule out tide 
levels reaching major, given the setup. 

For the rest of the NJ coast north of Barnegat Inlet, tide levels 
are currently forecast to reach Minor on Wednesday and Thursday.
